definitions.explanation: A proposal or tip presented as an easy way to make money. Usually carries a note of suspicion — the word most often appears in warnings about scams.

examples.japanese: うまい{儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}には{注意|ちゅうい}しよう。
examples.english: Be careful of too-good-to-be-true money-making schemes.

examples.japanese: {友人|ゆうじん}から{儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}を{持|も}ちかけられた。
examples.english: A friend approached me with a money-making proposition.

examples.japanese: {必|かなら}ず{儲|もう}かるという{話|はなし}を{信|しん}じて{投資|とうし}し、{結局|けっきょく}{大金|たいきん}を{失|うしな}った。
examples.english: He believed a scheme that promised guaranteed profits, invested, and in the end lost a large sum.

notes:
Composed of {儲|もう}ける (to make a profit) + {話|はなし} (story, proposal), with the sequential voicing that turns はなし into ばなし in compounds.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- うまい{儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}: a too-good-to-be-true scheme
- {儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}を{持|も}ちかける: to approach someone with a scheme
- {儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}に{乗|の}る: to go along with a scheme
- {儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}に{飛|と}びつく: to jump at a money-making offer

USAGE:
The phrase うまい{儲|もう}け{話|ばなし}はない ("there is no easy money") is a set warning, and police and banks use {儲|もう}け{話|ばなし} in fraud-prevention campaigns. Treating one as genuine usually needs an explicit qualifier such as {本当|ほんとう}の.
